Section 2: Individualization and Adaptation
If you have made it here, you have mastered threshold training at a high level.
You have delivered results, and you know your body well. Then it may be time for the next step. This section is not about fixing something that is broken.
It is about optimizing something that already works. We go deeper into how genetics, muscle fiber composition, and individual differences can affect how you adapt the model.
Genetics and Individualization
What if your body responds differently than expected to threshold training?
Through the years, I have observed something interesting. Even when everything is done correctly, intensity control, periodization, management of muscle tone, certain runners struggle with the model. Not from lack of will or under-standing, but because their genetic starting point is fundamentally different.
Genetics is probably central to this.
The first time this truly became clear to me was toward the end of 1999.
My second great childhood hero, alongside Sebastian Coe, was Vebjørn Rodal, Olympic champion from 1996. Before the 1999 season, his training shifted from a relatively intensive focus to somewhat more threshold-based work. I remember a proud sports director showing me his measurements during spring. The threshold numbers were better than ever. But the competition results? They dropped substantially relative to his level. What was the actual problem?
Rodal was probably more type II-dominant, explosive, fast, built for shorter, more intense loads. When some of his training was converted to longer, monotonous threshold sessions, part of what made him unique disappeared.
His threshold level improved on paper, while his race results declined. I have seen this pattern repeat itself.
Many runners thrive and flourish with long threshold sessions and high volume. Some tolerate it poorly, regardless of training experience or understand-ing. The difference most likely lies in muscle fiber composition.
There are recreational runner versions of Rodal as well. Perhaps you were someone who always thrived in childhood with explosive jumps or sports involving sprint elements. Iflong, monotonous threshold sessions drain you more than they build you up, it may be wise to reflect. It could mean your body responds better to slightly shorter intervals, more variation, and more frequent rests, within the same principles, simply because your muscular system functions best that way.

WARNING SIGNS THAT PURE THRESHOLD TRAINING MAY NOT SUIT YOU
*   You can complete threshold sessions technically correctly, but progression is absent over months
*   The muscular system feels constantly heavy, even on easy days and after sufficient rest
*   You experience repeated muscle and tendon injuries despite correct intensity control
*   Short, intense sessions feel natural and good; prolonged threshold work feels like a battle
*   You have a background in explosive sports or notice you have always been fast rather than enduring
Muscle Fiber Composition and Important Adaptations
Research shows that the distribution of muscle fibers varies enormously between individuals. Some have up to 80% type I fibers (endurance fibers). Others have 60-70% type II fibers (fast fibers). Those with a preponderance of type II fibers can struggle with traditional threshold training. These fibers are designed for short-term, high-intensity work rather than prolonged moderate load.
My own experience was that I lay somewhere in the middle of this spec-trum, but leaning toward type I. As a teenager I was fast I ran 60 meters in 7.2 seconds at 15, completely at the top of my age group in Norway. But I was more enduring than fast. I did not have a completely "pure" endurance-ori-ented muscular system. But precisely therefore, threshold training worked so well for me, It compensated for genetic limitations by maximizing the aerobic system, the ability to use oxygen effectively over extended time. I had enough type I fibers to allow that, with further adaptation.
One can say that these qualities are partly trainable. Studies also show that athletes who have trained for many years with endurance work adapt accord-ingly, including changes in fiber composition. The total picture is therefore somewhat complicated. Should you give it a proper chance and aim to achieve such an adaptation, even it you suspect you are a more explosive type? Or should you account for this from the start? I think both approaches are possible.

ADAPTATIONS FOR RUNNERS WITH A PREPONDERANCE OF TYPE II FIBERS (FAST FIBERS)
If you have always been more fast than enduring, the following adaptations make sense:
*   Cut the longest threshold sessions: Reduce both interval length and total volume. Long, monotonous threshold sessions will feel less effective and often degrade the qualities you already possess as a type Il runner.
*   Shorter easy runs: Use increased frequency instead. Volume can be maintained but divided up. Running pace should be kept consistently down.
*   More explosive elements: You tolerate and benefit more from sprint training and strength work.
*   Progressive threshold sessions: Reduce the number somewhat. They should be progressive, with increasing pace where you also increasingly allow yourself to go right over and through the threshold. Many also find good effect from a more explosive finishing focus, such as faster 45/15 or 30/30.
*   Periodic weeks without threshold focus: Every second or third week, allow yourself pure weeks without any threshold focus at all, to observe response and get a natural break from the monotonous pattern.
From Exception to Rule
The above was the exception, those who must adapt because genetics do not hit the model. For pure type Il-dominant runners, it is not optional, but necessary.
Many in this category have already been selected out at an earlier point, since endurance training never felt
"right" to begin with.
But what about everyone else? Those who master the training model focused on threshold work, deliver results, and thrive with the structure? For you, there is room for something different: a bit more experimentation within the framework, not because the model does not work, but because you may be
ready to go a step further.

Areas for Individual Adaptation and Experimentation
PREREQUISITES FOR EXPERIMENTATION
Before you begin experimenting, you should have three things in place:
1.    You have mastered threshold training. It sits.
2.    You have delivered results with it over time.
3.    You manage the transition from threshold-based base training to com-petition-sharpened work in summer.
If you have that foundation, these areas are interesting to explore: testing the X-session and "the two horses," race-pace specificity for volume through rest manipulation, the competition season, and double threshold variants.
The X-session and "The Two Horses"
The traditional X-session in the model is hill training. The choice is not random.
Hill running provides a high degree of muscular innervation, meaning you recruit a large portion of the muscular system.
You also get a strength element that occurs within the running movement itself, rather than through lifting weights or other forms of strength training.
At the same time, effort time is limited to 20-30 seconds, which means you avoid excessive accumulation of load within each interval. But here there are great opportunities for adaptation, and probably large individual differences.
Practical tip: If you can limit yourself to one day per week where you experiment with greater load, you can freely be creative in how you solve it. Either by improving qualities you experience as weaknesses, for exam-ple, the ability to float at race pace, or alternatively by strengthening qualities you are already good at but that lie above the threshold.
An example: you feel you do not get enough training at actual race pace. The X-session can be used to accumulate volume at race pace or above. To limit the load on the muscular system and avoid excessive muscle tone rise after the session, rests are used deliberately. The result is higher speed, but with longer and ideally running rest periods between the intervals.
Running rests in this setting provide a double effect: increased normalization oflactate and pH in the muscular system, and a muscle tone-lowering effect.
But all training beyond threshold work and easy running must be prioritized carefully. It likely carries risk beyond the load itself.
The Two Horses
The risk with more intensive training combined with threshold work I usually describe with an analogy, with permission to use data from Leif Olav Alnes.
Karsten Warholm, world record holder at 400 meters hurdles, runs once per week through large parts of the training cycle with 20 × 2 minutes of lac-tate-controlled threshold training. The 400 meters hurdles is perhaps the most demanding anaerobic event that exists. These sessions are done especially from autumn toward winter.
Anaerobic refers to the part of the energy system that contributes more when intensity becomes so high that aerobic processes alone cannot cover the energy demand. You get faster energy production, lactate rises more quickly, and you can only maintain the speed for a limited time.

The extremely interesting thing is this: As soon as Karsten begins running more anaerobic and very intensive training sessions through winter, it is almost like pressing a button. Lactate data shows that on these 20 × 2-minute sessions, his body begins far earlier to choose an anaerobic pathway, with rapidly rising Lactate, without it really being explainable in any straightforward physiological way. The change happens too quickly for that.
In a sense, the body faces a choice: At high load and needing to move as fast as possible, which a competition or tough training session essentially is, it will choose the energy system that feels most rational to activate.
The body can choose the aerobic horse, the enduring system where the body uses oxygen effectively, or the anaerobic horse, the explosive system where the body produces energy without sufficient oxygen. The instruction about which horse is best to bet on comes from the training in the preceding period.

This choice probably happens almost instinctively. If the anaerobic system has recently been activated and feels like an available solution path, the body will choose it-but too early if the need is prolonged effort.
For distance running, this is especially unfortunate, and I believe this is a key to understanding the phenomenon.

The Balance Point
Personally, I believe that the X-session, used year-round and in limited amounts, provides just enough load in the anaerobic area without triggering this unfortunate pathway too strongly. The button is not pressed hard enough. By doing it consistently over time, you also avoid an abrupt transition that can set this system going too quickly and intensely.
At the same time, you need some load on the muscular system beyond threshold training at the level this chapter covers. Hill training works well. It you tolerate it, speed training or fast strides after some sessions can also be tested.

It must be balanced against injury risk, but the benefit is that you accustom the body to recruiting more muscle fibers, without necessarily activating the unfavorable processes.
The Principle of Drip Load
Following from this, we have something I call drip load. This is an even more refined way to include the elements you want without simultaneously disrupting the pathway the body chooses.
You select the desired load and press the button regularly, but always in limited doses. You get sufficient but not excessive activation. Through these drips of load, you manage to capture roughly eighty percent of the effect without negatively affecting any of the other important qualities.
You therefore center around a threshold-oriented focus but harvest small
drips of other qualities regularly, but never too much.
EXAMPLES OF DRIP LOAD:
*   150-180 meter faster intervals on track in connection with a hill session or 45/15: you choose 1-3 rather than 5-8
*   3-5 plyometric jumps on stairs in 2-3 series with long rests after a threshold session. Finish with some light strides to lower muscle tone The principle: Press the button regularly, but never long enough that the body prioritizes the other system.
Drip load becomes in many ways the opposite of conventional thinking. You try to avoid the body training too hard on what you present, rather than deliberately pushing it. You present, introduce, drip it in, extract some benefit, but without maximum effect, then switch off.
Drip load before sessions
Placing drip load before the main session may be even more favorable than adding it afterward. You would start the session with the drips, before going into the planned training, for example threshold work. This is purely theoretical, but in animal studies there is support that the order, and especially the final load, can tip the signal balance one way or the other in a composite training session (Ogasawara et al., 2014). That is, the body reads what comes last and adjusts the adaptations accordingly in the period that follows.
Key point: Even though l am a proponent of running easy on easy days, I know that some try speed, strength, or plyometrics on "easy" training days. If you want this and want to add drips there, consider doing this as the very first load of the day.
Example:
*   Monday: Double threshold
*   Tuesday: Light warm-up, then short speed training as a drip, then easy morning long run as planned
The argument here is:
*   You concentrate drip load toward the day before
*   You go right into the normal load actually planned for Tuesday, the easy long run

*   The easy long run comes last and gives the body the right signal about what the day is about Drip load is a powerful tool for introducing varied loads without undermining threshold training. You get roughly eighty percent of the effect from speed, plyometrics, or strength without degradation. The key is consistency and limitation: press the button regularly, but never long enough that the body prioritizes the other system. But this raises a natural question. If we should constantly limit how much we train above the threshold, how do we become comfortable with the pace we will actually race at? Drip load gives us short glimpses of higher speed, but not enough time to truly acquire race pace in the body. If you are going to run 5K fast, the muscular system needs to know that pace. But as we have seen, it you train too much at race pace, you activate the anaerobic system too often, and your threshold capacity weakens. The dilemma is real.
You need some of that race pace, but you cannot add hard training at that pace week after week. Then the body eventually chooses the wrong horse, and because training at race pace most often carries an overly intensive character thar limits itself, 1 believe we actually know little about the real potential with large amounts of that type of training at race pace, but with lower intensity.
For many, I believe there is untapped potential within the model described in this book. How to solve this?

From Base Training to Competition Season
The methods we have now discussed, threshold training, double threshold, 45/15, drip load, and race pace with dynamic rests, work excellently in base training. But what happens when you are actually about to start competing?
How do you adapt the training model when competitions come close together, and when the body needs to be sharp rather than building fitness?
This is a question I get often. How does the training model relate to competition season and the transition there?
Competition Season: Maintenance Rather Than Building
I have touched on this earlier: the transition must be careful. Throughout, it is about carrying qualities from one phase to the next. If you lose too much of the threshold foundation because you emphasize too many intensive ses-sions, and if the muscular system also tightens up, you get little return on winter's foundation.
Put bluntly: Speed belps you little if you are 200 meters behind when the sprint starts.

In competition season, training will be event-dependent, but most manage with two simple threshold sessions per week rather than the traditional four sessions of 2 x double threshold in winter, if you train at a high level. This is more than sufficient for most over several weeks, possibly with shorter breaks in competition season where you add blocks with more threshold training.
Maintenance is the primary focus, together with competition-specific load.
Use of lactate meter in competition season
On intensive sessions: If you have access to a lactate meter, the curve through the session is interesting on all intervals over 800 meters. Experience indicates that shorter intervals, from 200-300 meters, give a somewhat poorer picture of the balance between aerobic and anaerobic qualities from the session alone.
The central thing is therefore to follow the lactate curve on longer intervals, especially intervals around 800-1000 meters. After two to three of these intervals at your 3000-5000 meter pace, the curve will flatten out if the aerobic engine manages to load maximally. But often it tips over into further rise if the anaerobic engine takes over too quickly.
Four days before my personal best at 5000 meters, I ran the following session: 4-6 x 1000 meters, followed by some faster 300-meter intervals. The times on the 1000s were 2:32.8, 2:32.3, and 2:32.3. Lactate was 6.8, 9.7, and 10.3 mmol/L. Here we see precisely the flattening I am talking about. Between interval two and three, the curve settles nicely and stably around 10.0 mmol/L and stays there for the rest of the session.
Double Threshold: A Continuation
I mentioned that in the competition period it is natural for many to reduce the double threshold work. But there is room to experiment here. It is possible to use double threshold in competition season-not to maximize the amount of

You choose frequent but non-demanding sessions for maintenance, without actually focusing on building them further.

The double threshold study coming up in the next chapter shows this directly-two divided threshold sessions producing less load than one long session.
You can use double threshold in two ways:
1.    First, to accumulate as much volume as possible on threshold training
2.    But you can also choose to use it to limit the load while preserving the threshold speed
In summer and competition period, the latter principle can be used. If you choose to add, for example, one day with double threshold that is a bit lighter than usual, you can allow yourself more easy training days after a competition or harder training session.

In the winter of 1996, I was training with Peter Coe during one of his "top-up mileage weeks" —periods where he compressed conditioning work into a short block to compensate for phases with lower mileage. The schedule happened to include two threshold sessions on the same day. It was not presented as a revolutionary concept. It was simply how that particular week was organized.
But something about it stayed with me. The morning session felt normal.
The evening session felt different, not harder in the way I expected, but more responsive, as if the earlier effort had prepared the ground for something. I kept coming back to it.
At Indiana University in 1997, training under Sam Bell, I found myself adding extra threshold work beyond what the program prescribed. The official afternoon session would end, and I would wait until darkness had settled over campus before slipping out to run more intervals alone. I may be the only athlete ever reprimanded for unauthorized threshold compliance!
In Norway, I spent time observing Leif Olav Alness sprint group. Hour after hour, they accumulated work in concentrated blocks. Effort, rest, effort, rest. All day. Then recovery. Alnes had figured out something fundamental: the body does not need endless spacing between hard sessions. It needs intelligent clustering, load concentrated into receptive windows, followed by genuine rest.
Since that first experience with Coe, 1 continually fine-tuned the approach.
Two threshold sessions on the same day, separated by six to eight hours, then complete recovery. The method evolved across nearly a decade of testing, trying variants, later measuring lactate responses, correlating how sessions felt with what the numbers showed, discarding what failed, refining what worked.
What began as almost an incidental detail became a deliberate structure Today it is used by Olympic champions and elite programs worldwide, and increasingly by serious recreational runners.
This chapter covers where the idea came from, why it works physiologically and how you can integrate it safely into your own training.
The Basic Principle
Think of studying for an important examination. You could sit with the material for six hours straight, but after three or four your concentration fractures. You find yourself reading the same sentence repeatedly, absorbing nothing. The mind has stopped processing new information-and continued effort yields diminishing returns.
Or you could split the work differently. Three hours in the morning when your head is clear, a genuine break in the middle of the day doing something entirely different, then three hours more in the afternoon when concentration has returned. Total study time remains the same, perhaps even increases. But the quality of learning is entirely different. You absorb more, retain more, and finish less depleted.
Double threshold operates on the same logic. The body maintains quality through two focused sessions, not by grinding through one long session of scattering hard efforts across too many days with incomplete recovery between each. You complete the work while the system is receptive, rest while the deeper recovery processes unfold, then return fresh for the next training block.
Here is what the researchers at NTNU discovered in their 2024 study: the body actually responds more favorably to two shorter threshold sessions than to one long one. Heart rate runs lower, lactate accumulation stays more con-trolled, and recovery needs diminish, all while total training volume remains
the same or increases.

NTNU STUDY: KEY FINDINGS
Single long session (6 × 10 min): During the 6 × 10-minute session, researchers observed cardiovascular drift, a gradual increase in heart rate, lactate, and perceived exertion through the workout. The second half showed 2.8% higher heart rate and 0.41 mmol/L higher lactate than the first half. Athletes reported feeling noticeably more fatigued toward the end.
Two shorter sessions (2 × 3 × 10 min): When the same athletes split the identical workload into two sessions with 6.5 hours between, heart rate and lactate actually dropped in the second session: 2.5% lower heart rate, 0.58 mmol/L lower lactate compared to the first session. Athletes felt good during both sessions and reported less muscle soreness the following day.
The study examined acute responses rather than long-term training adaptations, so it cannot tell us directly how these differences compound over months. But it confirms an important point: load can be organized more effectively.
Does lower strain mean smaller training effect? This question sits at the core of the double threshold philosophy.
The goal is not maximum strain per session, but to accumulate high-quality work within a concentrated window, then allow the body to recover fully before the next block.

The result is two things. First, you double the training load within that defined time window. Second, you allow training blocks on separate days to have sufficient spacing, and therefore recovery.
If you can complete 4-6 hours of threshold work per week using double threshold versus 2-3 hours with traditional spacing, while recovering just as well or better, who wins over time? This is obviously valuable for competitive athletes, but what about recreational runners?
Relevance for Recreational Runners
"But I'm not an elite athlete..." No, perhaps not. But that does not mean the principle is irrelevant to you. A common misconception holds that double threshold belongs exclusively to elite athletes, that you need to break 30 minutes for 10K before the approach makes any sense. The reality is more nuanced.
A practical example
Consider a runner who completes 10K in 45 minutes, with a threshold pace around 4:45-5:00 per kilometer (7:39-8:03 per mile). A traditional 40-minute threshold session at that intensity is genuinely demanding. Recovery may take days, and that entire week contains only 40 minutes of quality work performed with truly fresh legs.
But what if you split it up, with somewhat more careful sessions than an elite athlete would use? Twenty minutes of threshold running in the morning on your way to work, perhaps 6 × 3-minute intervals. On the way home, 20 × 1 minute. Same total volume, but fresh enough for easy running or rest the following day, before another hard session two days later. Over the course of a month, total threshold volume can double.
Why the Muscular System Allows It
Here we encounter an apparent paradox. You would think two intensive sessions on the same day would be more demanding than spreading them across several days, especially for recreational runners. There is logic to this, recovery is measured in hours and days between efforts. But double threshold is
an exception.
The limiting lactor in running is the muscular system. Muscle soreness and clevated muscle tone set in primarily on the day or days after hard training, not
to this timing.

By completing two hard sessions on the same day, you concentrate load within a receptive window. You thereby limit the number of days per week with muscular soreness and elevated tone, relative to the number of hard sessions completed. Training effect rises while injury risk, for many runners, actually falls.
Think of it this way: double threshold is really one long session with a long break in the middle. That framing is perhaps the most important understanding of why the model works.
Fitting It Into Daily Life
Double threshold can solve the puzzle of a hectic weekly schedule with creative planning. Suppose you manage four to six running sessions per week, two or three of them at threshold intensity. Daily life is demanding, work drains your energy, limited surplus after the workday, but weekends offer more flexibility.
One option is to place both threshold sessions on Saturday or Sunday, limiting yourself to just one threshold session during the workweek. You can even place the two sessions close together, with only a few hours between.
Personally, I often chose six to eight hours between sessions, but down to two or three hours can work for many.
Although it may seem intense, you achieve several things:
*   You run with more surplus when sessions are placed on days with less competing stress
*   You accumulate intensity over a shorter period, providing more recovery time the rest of the week, especially favorable from a muscular perspective
*   You create an adaptation effect where the body adapts specificaly to a different type of stimulus than the rest of the training week, which can lift you to a new level
In such a recreational setup, 1 still recommend that the first session consists of somewhat longer intervals, while the second session has shorter intervals from 30 seconds to 1 minute.
Level-Specific Approaches
Here we must be practical. Double threshold looks different for different run-ners. Treat it as something extra if you are injury-free and already have good control of your training.

Warning: I advise against this training approach if you do not have:
*   Complete control of intensity around the threshold
*   Been completely injury-free over time
*   Experience tolerating double sessions in general
*   Discipline to refrain if it does not feel right
Without this foundation, I advise against this training approach, the risk becomes too high relative to the benefit.

How to apply it in practice
The Morning Session
The morning session is the key to the entire system. Be careful, execute it wrong, and it impacts the evening session. Execute it right, and you initiate a cascade of physiological processes that prepare the body for round two.

Start with warm-up. Do not skip this before the morning session; the afternoon session is more straightforward. The warm-up should be a kind of check-in after the night, especially to sense whether you have small injuries or aches that need consideration. If you run with a heart rate monitor, check your warm-up heart rate during a short 3-5 minute warm-up. You can then use both resting heart rate and warm-up heart rate to monitor your body's rest and receptivity status.
The actual threshold work starts 5-10 seconds per kilometer (8-16 seconds per mile) slower than planned threshold pace. Let the body find its rhythm.
After 5-10 minutes, increase to target pace if it feels right. You run yourself into pace, more with this type of early morning session than other training sessions.
You adjust yourself gradually into a day of active training at the correct intensity.
What do you do during the break between sessions? Work, eat, rest. But I recommend avoiding physically demanding activity on your muscles. Standing physical work between two threshold sessions can be provocative muscularly and increase injury risk. So if you have a generally physically demanding job, you should be careful about adding double threshold on workdays.
Pace on the Morning Session
I sit here at the desk looking at the pile to my right. 5,500 lactate tests with curves. Ring binders, loose sheets, and notes scribbled all over the margins.
When I leaf through them now, the pattern is so clear it almost becomes comical.
The morning session with double threshold runs significantly slower. Always.
There are three reasons for this. Longer intervals lower pace in themselves. For most people, the body performs worse in the morning, body temperature is lower, muscles are stiffer, and nervous system response is slower than later in the day. And the morning session provides a muscular preparation effect that helps the evening session.
When I add these three effects together, I see it again and again, a gap of approximately 10-15 seconds per kilometer (16-24 seconds per mile) between
6-minute intervals in the morning and 1-minute intervals in the evening. My
old training partners measured the same.
This summarizes the most common mistake I see in double threshold: too
hard a morning session.

Surprisingly the afternoon session often feels better than the morning. But do not fall into the trap, it is still important to start disciplined, because the bodys response can differ from the morning. The NTNU researchers found lower lactate levels in session two, but that does not mean you should push harder, I recommend holding the same subjective or measured intensity.
There is also room for adaptations here, and some are more extreme than others. This is from an email I received from an eager recreational runner that truly illustrates how the model can be used creatively:
"I have also established what I believe is 'double threshold for parents of small children.' I've tried it now for over a year and think it works very well. It is 4:30-5:30 AM, 3 × 10 min and then packed lunches and breakfast with the kids. Then from 7:00 to 8:00 AM, 10 × 1000 m, followed by school and daycare drop-off. It is 1.5 hours between sessions, but it works. If it gets shorter than that, it becomes too short (ideally 1:45 between seessions).
Recovery is significantly better by taking the second session in the morning than pushing it into the afternoon or evening. The muscular system is also often very good."
Something like this is recommended only for the especially interested!

Intensity and Frequency
Double threshold is not inherently dangerous when executed correctly. But a few things demand extra attention.
The biggest pitfall is, as mentioned, intensity set too high. You start the first session slightly too hard, perhaps just above your normal threshold pace, or a bit too aggressive for that day's form. "Feels fine," you think. But then the afternoon session comes, and the body has not recovered. You push to hold the same pace. Now lactate is far too high, and you struggle through with a muscular system that is poorly receptive.

You have just completed two hard sessions in one day, but triggered a series of unfortunate processes in the body that increase recovery requirements. The next training week becomes an accumulated load rather than increased adaptation and performance. Motivation fades, with increased risk of overtraining and injury.
The second major pitfall is setting the frequency too high, because double threshold is almost seductive. When it works, it feels too good to be true. You want to do it every day, but you should resist the temptation. For experienced recreational runners, I would say maximum one, perhaps exceptionally two double days per week. For sub-elite and elite, this can stretch toward two double days per week. It is important to remember that adaptation also happens during recovery, not just actively during training, and you must balance both to make progress over time.
Periodization
Double threshold is a tool with its time and place also in a larger perspective within an annual cycle. For many, this may be irrelevant it you train completely evenly year-round. But if you try to peak for certain competitions annually, you should consider the following:

DOUBLE THRESHOLD IN THE ANNUAL CYCLE
Preparation period (3-4 months): Double threshold has a large place here. Two double days per week for ambitious runners, none or one for recreational runners.
Competition preparation (2-3 months): Reduce the number of double days. Introduce more specific speed work.
Competition period (1-2 months): Maximum one double day per week, always with good distance to competition days.
Nutrition
What about nutrition? Before the first session in the morning, individual pret-erences apply. Some perform best fasted, others need some fuel. Personally, I always run fasted on morning training, regardless of how intensive it is, both now and during extremely hard long threshold sessions at altitude in Eldoret, Kenya. There can be good arguments for this, as you get an extra training stimulus from training with a fasted body.
Between sessions, you have two options. If you are building toward a marathon, it can actually be worthwhile to train running nearly fasted into the second threshold session. This is to train the body to run with somewhat emptier energy stores, which is the case toward the end of a marathon. But if you are not in such specific preparation, get carbohydrates and protein in a 3:1 ratio within 30 minutes after the morning session. Lunch should have some substance but not be heavy.
Atter the second session, you can relax a bit, a proper meal within 2 hours, with protein for muscle repair and carbohydrates to refill energy stores.
Individual Differences
After years of practical experience and increasing research interest, there are still gaps in our understanding of double threshold. One observation is that some respond even better than others.

Sex differences
Preliminary observations may suggest that some women respond differently to double threshold, and that it may be cycle-dependent. Estrogen levels in the body affect both which energy sources you use during training and how quickly you recover. Therefore, where you are in the menstrual cycle may also matter for when it is most favorable to place the hardest sessions. But solid research is lacking here. I suspect that periodization of load will increasingly become cycle-dependent, also for this type of session. More on this comes later in the book, where I address cycle variation.
Age
Does double threshold work for veterans? Intuition says that older athletes with reduced recovery capacity may benefit greatly from the method by getting longer time between training blocks, again, if we think of double threshold really as just one long training session with a long break in between. But a number of factors, including muscle elasticity, change with age, so it is with great uncertainty that I write this. It can potentially increase injury risk, and I think that careful adaptation is extra important.
Muscle fiber composition
Finally, and perhaps most importantly: are there pure genetic components that matter? Is it the case that "slow" runners with a predominance of type I muscle fibers (endurance fibers) experience greater effect from and tolerate doubling better than more explosive runners? Or do the same principles apply, but with a somewhat different composition of the training sessions themselves?
It is likely that more explosive runners should have somewhat more elements of 45/15 sessions rather than the longer continuous runs/intervals typ ically recommended as morning sessions for double threshold. We definitely do not have the answers here, which is why individual testing and adaptation remains highly relevant. If you want to learn more about this and what type of runner you are, it is discussed further in Chapter 6, where muscle fiber composition is specifically described.

Psychological Benefits
Double threshold is not just physiology, but also psychology. When you have two sessions, neither session becomes so "important." Did you miss a bit on the morning session? You get another chance in the afternoon. Completing two quality sessions in one day builds confidence. "If I can do this, what more am I capable of?" The mentality spreads to the entire training cycle, not just
the next session.
The increased planning that double threshold requires has an interesting side effect. You must organize the day better, prioritize sleep, and plan meals.
Many find that these habits improve their entire lifestyle, not just their train-ing. Paradoxically, runners often report performing best when life is otherwise structured, with work or studies providing fixed frameworks. When you have limited time and must be efficient, training also becomes more focused. Structure breeds structure.
My own experience was that I also performed best during periods with full study load. When daily life was structured and I had to plan well, training also worked better. When I instead tried to commit fully without those same frameworks, the rhythm often disappeared.
The Foundation Is Correct Intensity
Double threshold is a powerful tool when used correctly, but still just one of many tools. Success in endurance sports still comes from continuity, patience, and intelligent progression. And not least, double threshold is part of a thresh-old-based training focus, where you must focus on the correct intensity for the model to work.
Still, for many it represents a shift in how we think about training load and recovery. From "no pain, no gain" to "optimal dose, maximum response.
From volume for volume's sake to strategic accumulation of quality work. be patient, listen to your body.

Key point: Double threshold is not for everyone, and it is not for every training period. It is not a quick fix for poor base training or lack of con-tinuity. But for those who are ready, who have built a solid conditioning base, who have time and motivation to structure the day around train-ing, who can resist the temptation to push too hard, and who have been running injury-free over time, double threshold can be one of the most effective things you can do.
Limitations and the Next Step
After more than two decades with threshold training, I have learned that there is no single perfect formula. What works for your training partner may not work for you. What worked for me at 25 does not always work now at 47. But the basic principles remain the same. Intervals beat continuous. Variation beats monotony. Systematic work over time beats extreme individual sessions. And most importantly, threshold training is not the goal in itself—it is a means to become a better runner.
Still, after thousands of hours with threshold training at all levels, I have observed some interesting limitations. Even the most dedicated threshold runners eventually reach a point where progress stagnates for most, not because threshold training has lost its effect, but because the body needs a change in stimulus to take the next step. For some this takes longer than others, surprisingly long, but the point usually comes sooner or later.
Three challenges
The first challenge is time efficiency. Many recreational runners, especially those with limited training time, struggle to get enough volume for pure threshold training to give optimal effect. 30-50 minutes per week of threshold training can provide good progress, but the body has capacity to respond to more if the training is smart enough. In addition, running volume in itself is one of the most important factors for progress.
The second challenge is speed adaptation. Threshold training takes place in a relatively limited speed range. Over time, this can lead to what I call speed stagnation, you become very good at one type of movement but lack the adap tation required to take the next step. I still maintain that threshold training itself is most important, but this is an element that stretches the framework just enough.
The third challenge is mental monotony. Even the most enthusiastic runner can tire of endless rounds of 6 × 6 minutes. Variation in interval lengths helps, but is not always enough to keep motivation up and focus sharp over months and years. At the same time, variation must be implemented without destroying what threshold training builds.
A somewhat different solution
How to solve this? The answer did not come from traditional interval research, but from the boundary area between physiology, neurology, and what can be called metabolic flexibility. The inspiration came from several sources: research on soccer players who naturally performed repeated high-intensity runs with short breaks, Professor Véronique Billat's work on maximizing time at VO_max, and systematic experimentation over a long time on myself.
